segments.text: Hi, it's Norman Swan here. Before I let you get to this week's health report, I want to give you a personal recommendation for another great podcast from Radio National. Indeed, a show I hosted for about five years. It's Life Matters. It delves into what makes humans tick, not sick, but tick. And it's life, not always as you know it. So look for Life Matters on the RN website, ABC Radio app, or wherever you listen to podcasts. But now, here comes the health report.
Hello and welcome to this week's Health Report with me, Norman Swan.
Today, behavioural activation, a simpler, cheaper form of psychotherapy for depression.
How to make our healthcare system, especially our hospitals, safer?
Could Victoria show us the way after a disaster in one of their maternity services?
And cervical cancer, cancer in the neck of the uterus, is a nasty malignancy which is hard to treat,
but luckily it's preventable by screening.
For many years, Australia has been a world leader in cervical cancer screening,
using the so-called pap smear, looking for rogue cells under the microscope.
The result has been very low rates of invasive cervical cancer by international standards.
But from next year, cervical cancer screening will undergo a radical change,
and some have asked whether it will be safe.
A paper in this morning's Medical Journal of Australia has tried to answer that question,
and one of the authors, Karen Canfell of the Cancer Council in New South Wales,
is in the studio with us, as is Jonathan Carter, Director of Gynaecological Oncology at the Chris
O'Brien Lifehouse Cancer Centre in Sydney. Welcome to the Health Report, both of you.
Thanks, Tom.
Thanks, Norman.
Jonathan, what are the changes from next year?
Well, up until now, the PAPSME screening system, which originated back in the 1990s as a national
and coordinated approach, involved PAPSMEs for women aged from 18 onwards every two years.
and whilst that has been a great step forward
with a reduction in the incidence of about 50%
in patients developing cervical cancers,
that incidence has plateaued over recent years
and so the current recommendations
which will be coming to effect in May of next year
involves a test called the HPV test
which is kind of like from the pap test,
it's not a blood test.
So you're scraping the cervix as well?
So the women's will still need to have a scrape of the cervix, but instead of having a smear performed,
the laboratories will look for the DNA of the HPV virus, which we now know is the causative agent for cervical cancer.
So every five years, women will be invited to have an HPV test.
From the age of 25?
from the age of 25. And if that HPV test is positive, they'll have a reflex smear and
colposcopy. And so the difference apart from the HPV testing, so it's every five years? Yes.
And it's by invitation. So at the moment, unless you've got a really good GP who has a system for
recall, it's up to the woman to actually remember to go along to have her smear. Yes, that's correct.
So the worry is younger women, maybe you're neglecting younger women. There's the issue of
interval cancers. If it's already five years, are you going to get developed cancer
in between times? And it's the younger woman, Karen, that you've been looking at
in the study in this week's Medical Journal of Australia. Tell us about the study.
Well, that's right, Norman. So what we've done is on the threshold of these major changes,
we've done a 25-year look back, essentially. So we looked at the performance of the National
Cervical Screening Program in women of different ages over the time since the program was initiated.
So that's 1988 or something like that.
Yeah, from the late 80s.
The program was initiated in 91.
And we looked at the performance of the program over 20 years.
And we found...
And just a back-to-back way of background,
we've probably been over-testing even by pap smear standards
because what Finland's been doing once every three years for a long time
and they've got lower rates than us.
That's right.
And in fact, the international recommendations are to screen
only every three years in younger women with pap smears
and to start at age 25 even with pap smears.
But when we suggested that in Australia, there was World War III with a pathologist and some gynecologist.
Well, I think what's changed is a couple of things.
First of all, the emergence of major international evidence on the greater effectiveness of HPV DNA testing.
It's a much more sensitive test.
And secondly, the impact of the HPV vaccine, which has been huge.
And we've seen this collapse of HPV infections in younger women.
So when you analysed the data by age group over the last nearly 30 years, what did you find?
So we found that there's been this great reduction of 50% or more in women over the age of 25.
And in fact, that reduction holds over beyond the age of stopping screening.
So we found this similar reduction even in women over the age of 70 who aren't targeted
by the screening program.
So that's fantastic.
It shows that there's long-term holdover benefits from regular screening.
But we found that there were no changes in rates in younger women under the age of 25.
So screening made no difference to you?
Screening made no difference over the 20-year period.
So the good news in that is that starting at 25 is not going to make any difference in theory.
But why is it not making any impact?
Well, the new program, first of all, to say it's predicted to be 20% even more effective than the current program.
So there's that.
Okay, that's the PR.
But let's go to what I'm being cynical.
But I mean, just tell me why under the 25 it had no impact.
Is that a different kind of cancer or what?
Well, there's a few reasons.
And it is consistent with a lot of international evidence.
I mean, first of all, cervical cancer is very, very rare in that age group.
Secondly, we have a lot of evidence that the testing doesn't pick it up well.
It may be that there's a rare subtype of cancer that is more aggressive.
But we have a lot of data now that shows that screening makes no impact in that age group.
And I think the new study today just confirms that in Australian context.
So, Jonathan, this is in the context that this group of younger women are largely going to be immunised against HPV coming through.
So it's not a completely naive group.
The other finding...
Well, they'll be immunised currently with a four-valent of HPV.
So not against every HPV?
No.
So the current vaccine is only sort of effective against 70% of the HPV genotypes or strains.
There is another vaccine that has been released in the United States, which has nine strains,
which covers about 90% of the HPV.
So there's still a risk, even if you've been immunized?
Well, women who have been vaccinated are still required to be screened.
What about interval cancers? Because you even get them in mammographic screening for breast cancer.
You have your mammographic screening and then a cancer appears before your next screen.
Five years, are you likely to get...
Look, it's very uncommon, extraordinarily rare for there to be a rapidly progressing cervical cancer.
And greater than 99% of all cervical cancers contain HPV virus.
So if a woman is HPV negative, the risk for having pre-cancer is extraordinarily low.
And then developing cancer after that, remembering there's a large time between contracting the
virus to developing persistence, pre-cancer and then cancer.
So even going from pre-cancer to cancer, that is estimated to take seven to 10 years.
And what about pre-cancer in your study?
Interval cancer, I should say.
So we just looked at cancer outcomes,
but we've got a lot of international evidence now
that HPV screening protects for a long time.
And in fact, some countries are going to 10 yearly intervals in older women.
Now, the other thing that you discovered in your study
was there are a few different types of cervical cancer.
There's not just one type.
And there's another type, one we're talking about mostly,
is called squamous cell carcinoma.
And there's another one called adenocarcinoma.
It doesn't really matter what the names are.
Screening has not affected adenocarcinoma at all.
And I'm just wondering from either of you,
is HPV testing, they're both affected by HPV, is HPV testing going to affect adenocarcinoma?
Yeah, that's our prediction because 80% or more, in fact even more than squamous cell cancers
are caused by the HPV virus. So HPV testing and HPV vaccination is predicted to impact these in a
much more cognizant way than the pap smear screening program has been able to. And is that
because the adenocarcinoma is more inside the cervix and the scrape doesn't pick it up? Well,
there's a number of different reasons, Norman. The pap smear, whilst a great test, a good test
is not a great test. So it's not as accurate as some people think. It's scraping the cervix on
the outside of the cervix where the squamous lesions are. And it's less reliable. Everybody
knows that in picking up the glandular lesions, which are on the inside of the cervix. So yes,
there are lesions within the cervix that may not be reached by a standard pap smear. And the pap
smear itself, its accuracy is, we talk about sensitivity and specificities, as you know,
is in the order of 60 to 70%. So people... So you can miss a cancer when it's there.
Absolutely. And just finally, well, not finally, but are we going for, I mean, we've over-tested
women for cervical cancer in the past. I think that's a reasonable thing to say,
according to the evidence. Are we still over-testing? Could you get away with once
every 10 years for HPV testing?
Are we being super careful here?
I don't think there's any wrong with being super careful.
And it's a big step from two yearly to five yearly screening.
And I think like everything that's been done up until now
and with the current guidelines,
it should be evidence-based in our climate.
So participation rates, Karen,
in colorectal cancer screening are pathetic in Australia.
They're down about 32%, 33%.
I think Victoria may be up to about 36%.
and that's probably the best in the country.
And one argument for,
there are two arguments for why it's not very good.
One is people don't like the idea
of rubbing their poo on a test,
but equally women don't particularly like
having their pap smear done.
So that's one comparison.
And the other issue said
is that the federal government made a mistake
in taking control of the colorectal cancer program,
whereas cervical cancer is under the control of GPs
and they've made sure it works.
by making it invitation only or not by invitation are you taking control away from gps
who are at the heart of success some would argue at the heart of the success of a cervical cancer
screening program so we're certainly not taking control away from gps norman but the biggest
change at the moment is that we'll send a proactive invitation to the woman to screen on her 25th
birthday and then proactive invitations every five years thereafter so certainly that doesn't
take away from the GP's management, but it really means that we'll have a good central system in
place for reminding women. Jonathan? I agree, absolutely. And the role of gynecologists,
because gynecologists have been, like, you go and see your gynecologist for a checkup rather
than your GP, and gynecologists like to do the pap smear. What's the role of the gynecologist
in all this? Look, I think the majority of pap smears can, should, and are currently being done
by general practitioners, family practitioners, and that's where the most are done. When a smear
is abnormal, the HPV test is abnormal, that's when gynecologists are involved.
And is there any benefit at all for a woman who has missed out on HPV testing in adolescence
being HPV immunised?
HPV vaccinated.
Sorry, she's not been HPV vaccinated. She gets her first test at 25 and she's HPV negative.
Should she be vaccinated?
she should be screened. So the thing about vaccination is it's most effective when it's
given to pre-adolescents. So that's why the program has traditionally targeted the youngest
12 to 13 year olds with a catch up initially. But the thing that we really want to say is that
vaccination and screening have to work together. So whether vaccinated or not, a woman should be.
You haven't asked my question. She's HPV negative. Why shouldn't she be immunised?
Well, it's a very complex issue and the HPV test is based upon cells that are scraped from the
cervix. The relationship between that and her immune system having developed a natural immune
response is poor. 50% of people who are infected actually don't have an immune response. So if
she's going to be continually exposed to HPV, then she may derive some benefit from being vaccinated.
But it doesn't really tell her true HPV status in terms of her exposure to her life?
it will tell her what is going on in the cells on her cervix,
which is where the malignant transformation will take place.
It won't tell her what her immune status is.
So the beauty of the current, of the move to HPV screening
is that, in fact, it doesn't matter what a woman's past vaccination status is.
We'll be able to basically assess her risk
based on the HPV result that we find.
Thank you very much to you both.
to Karen Canfield, who's director of the Cancer Research Division,
Cancer Council in New South Wales,
and Jonathan Carter, who's director of gynecological oncology
at the Chris O'Brien Lifehouse Cancer Centre.
Thank you very much to you both.
You're listening to The Health Report here on RN,
ABC News Radio and CBC Radio across Canada.
Perhaps one in ten people in Australian hospitals
suffer a complication and half of those are avoidable.
And what we're talking about is anything from wound infections
to bone fractures to bed sores to drug side effects to death.
Victoria has been in the spotlight because of seven preventable deaths of babies in its
Gerwa maternity service and a finding that the Victorian Health Department's processes
were unable to detect problems with what's called clinical governance, where standards
of care in a hospital were not being monitored or acted upon appropriately, perhaps.
Hence a review of the safety and quality system in Victoria, which has been released in the
last few days.
It's called Targeting Zero, was chaired by Professor Stephen Duckett of the Grattan
Institute, who's in our Melbourne studio.
Welcome, Stephen.
Good evening.
So you did this review.
It wasn't of the Jarawa service because that's already been done
by the Safety and Quality Council and Professor Ewan Wallace.
So you were looking at the system in general.
Yeah, we were looking more broadly.
I mean, obviously, the report was stimulated.
The inquiry was stimulated by the Jarawa Health Service tragedy.
But we were looking at the overall system and the governance of the whole system.
And just to get the sense of this right, when things go wrong,
It's not usually because of a bad egg.
It's because the system goes wrong.
So we're not looking for a head on a stick here.
No, they're quite separate processes, including the Australian Health Professional Registration Authority that looks at those bad egg issues.
We were looking at the overall system governance, the processes, the information and that sort of thing.
So you weren't that kind to the Victorian Health Department?
Well, we were quite strong in our language.
There were, you know, these 11 potentially avoidable deaths.
And, you know, this is a tragedy.
And I would like to see that we learn from that.
So what do you think the main learnings are from your review?
Well, I think Victoria is right at the forefront of being well regarded as the most efficient state in terms of public hospital provision.
But other states have jumped ahead of Victoria in terms of quality and safety governance.
New South Wales has a much better infrastructure for governance of quality and safety following the Garling report, I think, a decade or so ago.
Queensland, much better systems of tracking and monitoring safety issues following the Patel-Bunderburg tragedy.
South Australia, better incident reporting system.
So other states are going ahead and Victoria hasn't kept up with them.
So what changes are you suggesting?
Well, we've got a number of them.
There's 180 almost recommendations.
But some of them are these things.
We want more clinical engagement.
The department wasn't using the skills, knowledge of clinicians as much as it ought.
We want more transparency.
We want to be publishing how hospitals are going, public and private, in terms of their safety and quality performance.
We want to have the health department being more supportive of health services and providing advice.
At the moment, every single hospital has to reinvent the safety and quality wheel,
and there's not as much sharing of knowledge and transmission of knowledge about what works across the health system.

Now, despite Victoria being proud of its system and its decentralized approach, it is unique in that I think there are something like 85 different health services in Victoria, whereas in New South Wales, it might be, I don't know what it is, 17, similar sort of number in Queensland.
So they've shrunk it down to bigger services.
And I think one of your findings was that in Victoria, you've got some very small services which don't really have the skills to look after themselves properly in terms of safety and quality.
Yes, and so we've proposed strengthening the boards.
At the moment, some of these boards have been in place,
the members have been on them for 20 or 30 years,
and they say there's no turnover, no new ideas coming through.
There's not an adequate process for ensuring that they've got the right skills.
I mean, at the moment, there's a tick box.
Do you have clinical governance skills or not?
Who knows what that means?
And so we're proposing major strengthening of the board-level clinical governance
because they're the ones that are legally accountable.
But let's talk about clinical governance
because the average listener listening to us now
wouldn't have a clue what we're talking about.
We're talking about clinicians sitting around a table
trying to look at events that might have occurred in the hospital,
then doing research into why that would happen
so it doesn't happen again.
And just anecdotally,
it depends on rather honest conversations occurring
which probably don't really occur.

So you're talking about engaging doctors more in this, but they're actually traditionally quite scared to bring this up with their colleagues, even people who you'd think are just big, bruisey orthopaedic surgeons and wouldn't be scared of anything, but they're actually scared of raising stuff with their colleagues.
Yeah, there's two paths we're really talking about.
One is these events, you know, the unusual, the sentinel events, as they're called, operating on the wrong body part or leaving something in the wound.
They're very unusual.
and they are investigated to death in a sense.
What we also need to be looking at is patterns of care.
To what extent are there more hospital-acquired infections
in your hospital, in your clinical unit,
in your orthopaedic unit than in the state average?
And unfortunately what's happened in Victoria
is the hospitals themselves don't have enough information
about what the state average is.
They even don't have good information about how they're tracking against their own history.
So by focusing on patterns, I won't say make the person irrelevant, but it gets you to focus more on the systems.
It gets you to focus on are there systematic things happening in this hospital that aren't happening in other hospitals.
You also say in your report, which would shock the average person, is that safety and quality doesn't have a high enough profile, either at a state level or at a hospital level.
Yes, as I said, Victoria is very proud of the fact that it's the most efficient state in terms of the public hospital system.
And they've strengthened their emphasis on safety and quality in recent years.
But the example I use is there's a performance assessment scale that's used to rank hospitals to track how they're going.
And at the moment, there are three dimensions to it.
Are you going on budget?
And that's worth 30% of the score.
And the second one is, are you going on budget?
And the third one is, are you going on budget?
Not quite as bad as that.
But the first one is, are you going on budget?
The second one is, how are you going on your waiting list?
And the third one is quality and safety.
And originally, that was only 15%.
And they've increased that to 40%.
But when I went around Victoria and said to people,
do you think it's the right idea that if you go better on budget,
you're allowed to go worse on quality and safety?
I couldn't find anybody who thought that was a good idea at all.
So quality and safety isn't...
It's got to sit there in its own right.
Yeah, it ought to be there in its own right.
It ought to be something that we focus on.
And it's not at the moment.
But to do this, you can't expect a single service,
even a large service like, say, Royal Melbourne or the Alfred,
you can't expect them to do a lot of this stuff by themselves.
The department's going to have to do a lot for them, aren't they?
Yes, exactly.
So what we're saying is there needs to be way more support from the department to these services.
And so, for example, in New South Wales, there's a portal that clinicians across the state can access,
which provides them with information about how they're tracking against their peers,
how they're tracking against the state average.
We don't have that in Victoria.
And so we need to be providing more support to the clinicians in our hospitals, big and small,
to help them address these important issues.
When there was a problem in Britain in a hospital in Staffordshire in the Midlands,
the big question in the National Health Service was how many more Staffordshires are there?
Do we know how many more Geroas there are in Victoria or indeed any other state in Australia?
Well, I think we're not as good.
I think some states are better than others in tracking what's going wrong
and in trying to identify the issues.
When I was in Queensland, this was one of the things we wanted to err on identifying things early.
And so we probably over investigated just to make sure that Bundaberg would never happen again or reduce to a small risk that Bundaberg happened again.
We haven't had that same focus in Victoria.
And I think that's what we need.
And just finally, Stephen, how much can other states learn from you say that other states are ahead of Victoria in some respects, but how much is this applicable to other states?
There are some national issues that we raise.
So, for example, there needs to be better sharing of information
between the registration regulation bodies and the health services
because, you know, we know that if a person, a doctor, for example,
has complaints against him or her,
they're more likely to have complaints against them in the future.
But we don't get that information.
It's secret squirrel business in the regulator.
And so we need to have much more sharing of information.
So there's some national issues that we touch on in that report.
Thanks very much.
Stephen, and that's available on the health department's website.
On the health department website.
Thanks very much, Moulin.
Stephen Duckett, who's head of the health program
at the Granton Institute in Melbourne.
You're listening to the Health Report here on our end with me, Norman Swan.
There's a form of treatment for depression called behavioral activation.
There's just been a fascinating trial published in The Lancet
comparing it to the standard psychotherapy for depression
called cognitive behavioral therapy.
And one of the authors of this trial is David Eckerts
from the University of Durham.
Welcome to the Health Report.
Hi, Anorm.
What is behavioural activation?
Behavioural activation, it's not a new treatment for depression.
It's been around a long time.
It has a view that depression is sat not necessarily as something wrong inside us,
but something that has happened that's cut us off from those things in our world
that are important or antidepressant to us.
And as that happens, if it happened to any of us,
we would feel down, it would affect our mood,
and sometimes when people feel down to cope,
they tend to put things off or shut down,
and when they shut down, they become further isolated from those things,
and thus the loop develops.
So behavioral activation is a relatively simple treatment
that aims at helping people understand that relationship
between what they do and how they feel,
and then look at changing what they do on a day-to-day basis
just with small gradual steps to put them back in touch with their things in their world that are healthy and antidepressant to them.
And in that way, subsequently, they change how they feel.
So we call that MBA, working from the outside in.
So what did you used to enjoy doing kind of an audit of things you used to have fun with that you're not doing now?
Yeah, it's a little bit more complicated than just fun.
I mean, it would be lovely to think we could live a hedonistic lifestyle.
Yeah, particularly going to the football if your team's not winning.
Yeah, yeah, yeah.
It's things that are valuable, that give us a sense of purpose or meaning in our day-to-day lives.
Now, some of that will be pleasure.
Some of it will be necessary to us.
Some of it will be things like going to work or communicating with family members.
And not all of it is pleasurable, but it's functional for us.
So BA is a contextual treatment.
It looks at depression as sat in the context of your life.
So I take it that the activation piece is not get up off your arse and stop feeling sorry for yourself?
No, not at all.
What BA does is, first of all, it explores that concept with people.
So you understand what the meaning of those activities were?
Yeah, yeah.
And then you understand how they've gone out of your life because they go out of your life often for a reason.
Things will have happened that will make it difficult to do those things.
So we explore that with somebody and then we get them to look at the relationship at the moment between what they're doing and how they're feeling.
And then we gradually work together to develop a plan, a thing called activity scheduling, to put people back in touch with that stuff.
And then you regularly monitor that and you do some, you look at blocks in that treatment and work out what people can do.
There's a bit of cognitive stuff in there as well.
You might think, well, I can't go and do that because everybody knows I've been depressed and they're going to think that I'm weak and hopeless.
And you've got to get beyond that negative thought as well.
Yeah, but it's fundamentally different to cognitive behavioral therapy.
So in behavioral activation, what we do is we're more interested in the consequence of thinking that way.
So we'll recognize how people kind of ruminate and think about things.
We all do that, and it's much, much worse if we're experiencing depression.
We get less into trying to challenge the meaning of that for an individual,
which is how cognitive behavior therapy works,
and we're much more interested in the consequence of that.
So it's, you know, when you started feeling that way, what did you do?
and and when you did that how did you feel and and was that in the longer term kind of more
benefit you know in the short term it you know people do things to take away distress but in
the longer term we look at how that keeps people where they are now i've said so long talking about
behavioral activation one was running out of time here to talk about your trial but essentially you
did a semi-random it wasn't really a randomized it was kind of a semi-randomized trial of comparing
behavioral activation with quite inexperienced therapists in other words they weren't sort of
PhDs in psychology versus a course of cognitive behavioral therapy. What did you find?
Well, it was a randomized trial. It was a completely randomized trial.
Participants were randomized, completely at random away from the control.
Oh, I thought you selected people to make sure that you had a balanced set of...
No, no. We made sure each group were balanced on a few kind of things, which is good quality
randomized control trial um and what we found was non-inferiority so we found that ba delivered by
non-specialists was non-inferior in any way to the current gold standard of cbt delivered by
therapists so does non-inferior mean just as good as well not not quite what is what you do is you
set an inferiority margin around uh on a measure and you would plan to get your new your new
treatment the ba within that margin of the gold standard because to get to prove something
is exactly the same you'd need an unfeasibly large study to do that and and you found it was
also significantly cheaper yeah we got about a 20 percent reduction in costs so i think what's
interested in this interesting in this study in a national institute for clinical excellent
excellence over here asked for this study to be done. But what's really interesting is
what we've shown is that a very effective psychological treatment can be delivered by
non-specialists to the same standards as specialists. And when we have difficulty
in access to psychological treatments, which I think is worldwide, you know, this could offer
some promise. Dr. David Eckers, who's clinical senior lecturer in the School of Medicine,
in Pharmacy and Health at Durham University in the UK. I'm Norman Swan. This has been
The Health Report, and I'll see you next week.
